newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Women's education key to Latin growth - Mrs. Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Women's education key to Latin growth - Mrs. Clinton.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton on Wednesday told Latin American first ladies they should foster education, especially of girls, if the region's fledgling democracies and market economies are to develop.

"Democracy cannot thrive or survive without educated citizens," the U.S. first lady told the sixth conference of first ladies of the Americas. The meeting will be followed by a weekend summit in Santa Cruz, 300 miles (500 km) southeast of La Paz, at which more than 20 Latin leaders and U.S. Vice President Al Gore will discuss the environment and economic development.

"In a fast-pace, highly competitive global economy, an educated population is vital to every nation's and every region's economic growth," Clinton said on the second day of the four-day meeting on women's and children's rights.

But she cautioned on her first visit to this Andean nation, one of the poorest on the continent, that girls, especially those from minorities, were being left behind. "Girls from indigenous and minority communities, including in my own country, are least likely to secure the education they need," she said. Bolivia's population is largely Indian.

"Girls must not be left in the margin, consigned to lives of poverty and ignorance," she said. "Educating girls is the best single investment we can make if we care about building strong democracies with vibrant free market economies."

Brazil's first lady, Ruth Cardoso, said the time was ripe for women to be more active in political and economic affairs. "I think the time when women were considered as just a particularly fragile and vulnerable social group is over," she said. "Although there are still some instances of this, today women in all our countries are key players for development."

Clinton on Tuesday visited the Andean peak of La Cumbre outside La Paz and stopped to talk to some of the thousands of women vendors in Colla Indian garb who fill the narrow sidewalks hawking everything from fruits to video cassettes.
The U.S. first lady also visited a health centre and a cooperative bank specialising in credits for the poor and talked to patients and loan beneficiaries.

On Wednesday, the last day of her visit to Bolivia, she participated in the signing ceremony for a $2.25 million U.S. grant to the Pan-American Health Organisation to fight maternal mortality in Latin America. She said 23,000 Latin American women will die this year of pregnancy-related causes.

"Five women die every hour. Since we came in this room, between 10 and 15 women have died," Clinton said. She said desperate women often risk their lives undergoing illegal abortions for lack of voluntary family planning.
Tuesday's session focused on efforts to combat family violence and give women a bigger say in political affairs.

The Santa Cruz meeting will focus on sustainable development, a principle approved by world leaders at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and generally defined as pursuing economic growth without harming the environment.

The leaders will discuss a wide array of issues linked to sustainable development including poverty, education, wider public participation on development projects, funding and the transfer of environmentally clean technology.

Communist-ruled Cuba, which is not a member of the Organisation of American States, the regional forum that helped organise the Santa Cruz meeting, was the only Latin country not invited to the meetings in Bolivia.
